text: I’ll model the fluid directly as a closed axisymmetric annulus. The three prescribed stations will be joined by smooth interpolating splines in an axial meridian, then revolved about the engine axis. I’ll first create a coarse tessellated preview and verify station radii numerically; after that I’ll export four named patches and mesh the enclosed volume.

A single quadratic Bézier through each set of three stations gives a deterministic smooth blend without adding extra axial breakpoints. Its control point is chosen so that the curve passes exactly through the mid-duct radius at half length; this is an explicit modeling assumption because the requested blend law was not specified. I’m checking the available curve constructor before creating the meridian.

I’ll now construct the closed meridian in metres and revolve it. The source boundary edges are explicitly named (`outer_edge`, `outlet_edge`, `core_edge`, `inlet_edge`) before revolution. The preview will show the coarse surface tessellation, and the printed checks evaluate the Bézier curves at the three requested stations.

The coarse section has the intended converging outer wall and the inner cowl’s smooth rise and contraction. I’ll inspect the four revolved faces by surface type, area, center, and normal so the source-edge-to-patch correspondence can be confirmed before export; no patch will be inferred merely from an overall bounding-box position.

The face order follows the four source meridian edges exactly: outer revolution, outlet plane, core revolution, inlet plane. Their normals also point outward from the fluid (outer radially outward, core toward the axis, outlet +x, inlet −x). I’ll bind those named faces, assert their expected geometric character and areas, then export all patches in one welded tessellation pass.

For the final surface I’ll use 0.5 mm chord tolerance, much finer than the planned ~25–30 mm coarse volume cells, so STL faceting will not control the geometry. All four STL files will come from one tessellation, preserving shared seams.

I’ll use `snappyHexMesh` because the exported closed patch union is the authoritative geometry and patch names can be preserved directly. The coarse background grid is 30 mm isotropic (30×32×32); the box extends beyond the closed air volume, and `locationInMesh = (0.10, 0.35, 0)` selects the annular fluid while discarding the exterior and core interior. This point is safely between the measured core and outer radii.
I’ll generate and inspect the background mesh first, before surface cutting.

The background mesh is exactly 30 mm in all directions with 32,768 cells. I’ll now cut/snap it to the four-patch closed annulus at the same coarse level; this is intentionally the first volume-mesh pass, before deciding whether refinement is needed.

`snappyHexMesh` stopped before changing the mesh because this OpenFOAM build requires minimal `fvSchemes` and `fvSolution` files even for meshing. I’ll add empty valid dictionaries; no solver settings or boundary conditions are being introduced.
I’ll rerun the previously blocked coarse cut-and-snap operation.

The coarse cut mesh has 10,123 cells and completed all mesher quality checks. I’ll now run the binding bare `checkMesh` and inspect patch counts and topology before deciding whether this coarse resolution is adequate.

The coarse mesh passes `checkMesh`, has one connected region and all four named patches. Its total volume (0.2746 m³) is within 0.7% of the exact CAD volume (0.27639 m³), appropriate for this first pass. I’ll now render the actual volume mesh with a cutaway so the annular topology and surface conformity are visually checked.
The OpenFOAM reader confirms 10,123 volume cells and four boundary blocks. I’ll display a half-section of the actual cells with edges visible and overlay the four patches in distinct colors.

The cutaway confirms the correct annular region, continuous core exclusion, and distinct end patches. The coarse mesh has only about 5–6 cells across the narrowest radial gap, so I’ll refine the final background spacing from 30 mm to 20 mm (48³ background cells, expected roughly 30–40k retained fluid cells). This is my mesh-resolution choice, not a user-specified dimension.
I’ll regenerate the refined background mesh.
The final background is confirmed at 20 mm isotropic spacing. I’ll cut and snap it to the annulus.
The final mesh contains 33,502 cells and the mesher reports no remaining quality violations. I’ll run the binding final `checkMesh` now.

The final mesh passes `checkMesh`: one region, four patches, 33,502 cells, maximum non-orthogonality 56.05°, maximum skewness 0.825, and no topology or geometry failures. I’ll preserve the exact CAD fluid volume as a STEP file alongside the required STL patches; the STEP remains in metres by construction.

The exporter signature reveals that its default STEP declaration is millimetres, so the preceding auxiliary STEP would be unit-labeled incorrectly even though the OpenFOAM geometry is correctly in metres. I’ll immediately overwrite that auxiliary file with an explicit metre unit; the STL and mesh are unaffected because they are unitless metre coordinates.

All deliverables are now consistent in metres. The exact requested station values were verified: outer cowl 0.450/0.430/0.410 m and core cowl 0.280/0.310/0.250 m at x = 0/0.450/0.900 m, each with zero interpolation error. The four-patch STL union is closed, consistently wound, manifold, and the final OpenFOAM mesh passes the binding check. No requested property remains unchecked.

The completion gate correctly notes that the meshing-side point was not recorded in the STL manifest, even though it was used by `snappyHexMesh`. I’ll re-export the unchanged four-patch tessellation with the same validated annular point `(0.10, 0.35, 0)` recorded in `patches.json`; this does not alter the already checked mesh.
The manifest now records the same inside-fluid point used to build the mesh. It lies at radius 0.35 m at x = 0.10 m, between the core and outer profiles. I’ll rerun completion checks without waivers.
